lesson.title: Tolerance: When the Brain Adjusts to the Drug
lesson.summary: Drug tolerance develops when repeated exposure causes neurons to reduce or desensitize their receptors, so a familiar dose produces a weaker effect over time.
lesson.body:
Drug tolerance is what happens when repeated exposure to a psychoactive drug causes the same dose to produce a weaker effect over time, so a person needs progressively larger amounts to feel what a smaller amount used to produce. Tolerance is not a sign of weak willpower or a psychological quirk. It is the direct, measurable result of the nervous system adapting to a chemical it keeps encountering.

Most of the drugs covered so far in this unit work by strongly activating a receptor, either directly as an agonist or indirectly by boosting how much neurotransmitter reaches that receptor. From the receiving neuron's point of view, a receptor being stimulated far more than usual, hour after hour, day after day, looks like a system running too hot. In response, neurons often reduce the number of receptors available on their surface, a process called downregulation, or make the remaining receptors less responsive to stimulation, called desensitization. Either change means the same dose of drug now has fewer or less sensitive targets to act on, producing a smaller effect than it once did.

Not all tolerance happens at the receptor. Metabolic tolerance can also develop when the liver responds to repeated drug exposure by producing more of the enzymes that break that drug down, clearing it from the bloodstream faster. Chronic alcohol use, for example, increases the activity of liver enzymes involved in processing alcohol, so a regular drinker may metabolize a given amount of alcohol more quickly than an occasional drinker does, on top of any changes happening at GABA receptors in the brain.

Opioid tolerance is a well documented example of this pattern. With repeated activation, mu opioid receptors downregulate and become less responsive, so a person who started on a modest dose for pain relief may eventually need a substantially higher dose to get the same relief. This creates a genuinely dangerous gap: tolerance to the pain relieving and euphoric effects of opioids tends to build faster than tolerance to their effect on breathing, which is one reason overdose risk can rise even as a person feels like the drug is working less well for its intended purpose.

Tolerance can also fall quickly once drug use stops, even after it took a long time to build. Receptor numbers and sensitivity gradually recover during abstinence, but a person's expectations and habits often do not update as fast. This mismatch is a major reason relapse can be so dangerous: someone who returns to a previously tolerated dose after a period of abstinence may be taking an amount their body can no longer handle, since the neuroadaptation that once protected them has partly reversed.

Tolerance sets the stage for the next two chapters. The same neuroadaptations that make a familiar dose feel weaker also help explain why the brain comes to depend on the drug being present, which is where addiction begins, and why removing the drug abruptly can leave the nervous system in an unbalanced state, which produces withdrawal.
